summary: This experimental document describes the design of a traceroute protocol for Information-Centric Networking. It covers how both the client and the forwarder operate. It is a product of the Information-Centric Networking Research Group.

plainLanguage.summary: Traceroute follows a package and tells where it stops. This one does that for networks that ask for things by name rather than by address.

subtitle: Discover paths through name-based networks the way traceroute maps IP networks.

tldr.problem: IP networks have traceroute to map routes by address. Information-Centric Networking (ICN) routes by name prefix instead, so network operators need a tool to discover which forwarders a packet will traverse and measure the delays at each hop.
tldr.mechanism: ICN Traceroute sends packets with a hop limit that decrements at each forwarder. When the limit reaches zero, the forwarder replies with its name and path information. Clients send packets with increasing hop limits to discover each hop in turn, similar to how IP traceroute works.
tldr.outcome: Network operators can diagnose ICN networks, discover multiple available paths towards a named object, test whether data is cached on the path, and measure latency. This helps with troubleshooting and understanding ICN deployment.

facts.label: Return codes
facts.value: 1 for forwarder match, 2 for application, 3 for cache hit, 4 for hop limit zero

facts.label: Key mechanism
facts.value: Hop limit decrement to discover path hops

today: RFC 9507 is an Experimental protocol published in March 2024 by the Information-Centric Networking Research Group. It represents the consensus of ICNRG on traceroute design for ICN networks. As an experimental RFC, it may evolve as the ICN community continues deployment and experimentation.

sections.title: From IP Traceroute to ICN
sections.content:
In traditional IP networks, traceroute discovers the route to a destination by sending packets with an increasing Time To Live (TTL) field. Each router decrements the TTL; when it reaches zero, the router responds, telling the client its address. By sending packets with TTL 1, 2, 3, and so on, the client learns the path one router at a time.

Information-Centric Networking (ICN) does not route to addresses; it routes to names. An Interest packet carries a name prefix, and forwarders route it towards any source that publishes under that name. In ICN, the same troubleshooting goal matters: network operators need to know which forwarders a packet traverses and how long it takes. This RFC defines an ICN Traceroute protocol analogous to IP traceroute, adapting the concept of hop limits for name-based routing.
sections.plainLanguage: In the old network, you ask "what is the path to this address?" In ICN, you ask "what is the path to this name?" Traceroute answers both questions by following the packet.

sections.title: How IP Traceroute Works
sections.content:
IP traceroute sends consecutive packets (UDP datagrams, ICMP Echo Requests, or TCP SYN packets) with a TTL value increased by one, starting at 1. The first packet expires at the first router, which sends back an ICMP Time Exceeded message. The second packet expires at the second router, and so on. This expanding ring search gradually reaches the destination. The client learns the path by collecting the responses and timing them.

This simple mechanism works because every IP packet has a source address, which the responding routers use to send replies back to the client.
sections.plainLanguage: You throw a ball and say "stop after 1 bounce." Someone catches it and says "I am here." You throw again and say "stop after 2 bounces," and the next person says "I am here." Eventually you reach your friend.

sections.title: New Challenges in ICN
sections.content:
ICN networks present four major differences that complicate traceroute. First, ICN names are variable-length hierarchical strings, not fixed-size addresses. Second, ICN Interest packets have no source address; responses come back by reversing the path, not by using a source address. Third, ICN supports multi-path, multi-destination forwarding; a single Interest name can retrieve data from multiple sources along different paths. Fourth, multiple Interests for the same name arriving at a forwarder can be aggregated in the Pending Interest Table (PIT), so the same request is forwarded only once.

The RFC defines goals for ICN Traceroute: trace one or more paths to an ICN forwarder by its administrative name, trace paths to named data objects, test whether a specific object is cached on the path and at which forwarder, and measure transit delays. The design uses packet encodings that diverge as little as possible from normal Interest and Data packets, allowing forwarders to distinguish traceroute requests from normal Interest packets while processing them similarly.
sections.plainLanguage: ICN is different from IP in four ways: names are not addresses, there is no source address, many sources can answer, and some packets get merged together. Traceroute needs to handle all of that.

sections.title: Packet Formats for CCNx and NDN
sections.content:
The RFC defines traceroute for two ICN implementations: CCNx and Named Data Networking (NDN), each with its own packet format.

For CCNx, a traceroute request is a special packet type (PT_TR_REQUEST) that looks like an Interest but includes a hop limit field and a Path Label TLV (from RFC 9531, which specifies path steering). The request message carries a name TLV with the target prefix and a nonce, a unique identifier to prevent Interest aggregation and allow clients to match replies to requests.

A traceroute reply (PT_TR_REPLY) looks like a Content Object but includes a Path Label TLV and a payload containing the sender's name, their signature, and a return code indicating why the reply was generated: because the forwarder matched the administrative name, because an application serves the prefix, because the object is cached, or because the hop limit reached zero.

For NDN, a traceroute request is an Interest packet with the target name, a nonce value, and the suffix "traceroute" appended. The reply is a Data packet with a MustBeFresh constraint and a freshness period of 1 to prevent caching. Both formats include the Path Label TLV to enable path steering in later requests.
sections.plainLanguage: A traceroute request is a special packet that says "when you process this, tell me who you are." A reply says "I am a forwarder named X." The nonce ensures each request is unique so it does not get merged with others.

sections.title: How Forwarders Process Traceroute Requests
sections.content:
When a forwarder receives a traceroute request, it decrements the hop limit. If the limit has not expired (is still greater than zero), the forwarder forwards the request upstream based on the Content Store lookup, PIT creation, longest-name-prefix-match FIB lookup, and any path steering value provided.

If the hop limit reaches zero or becomes zero, the forwarder generates and sends a traceroute reply downstream. The reply includes the forwarder's administrative name and signature, and the appropriate return code: 1 for administrative name match, 2 for application prefix match, 3 for Content Store hit, or 4 for hop limit reached zero.

A traceroute reply is final if one of three conditions is met: the target name matches the forwarder's administrative name, the target name exactly matches a Content Object in the Content Store (unless the client excludes CS hits), or the target name matches an FIB entry with an outgoing face leading to a local application. The client uses the return code to know when to stop sending traceroute requests with increasing hop limits and can then start a new traceroute session for a different path.
sections.plainLanguage: The forwarder counts down the hop limit. At zero, it says "I am here, named X." Otherwise, it passes the request forward to the next forwarder.

sections.title: Security and Privacy in ICN Traceroute
sections.content:
A reflection attack could occur if a compromised forwarder includes the name of a victim forwarder in its reply, redirecting future administrative traffic to the victim. To prevent this, the forwarder that generates a reply MUST sign the name in the reply's payload, so the client can verify the name is legitimate.

An on-path attack could involve a compromised forwarder modifying a reply it receives to replace the original forwarder's name and signature with its own. To foil this, a forwarder can sign the entire reply message, not just the name. The second approach adds computation cost and could enable denial-of-service attacks against forwarders.

To mitigate computation attacks, the RFC recommends handling traceroute processing in a separate management application running on the forwarder, isolated from the main forwarding engine. The second approach to locally scoped namespaces (prepending a routable prefix) introduces a risk of interest flooding amplification because the border forwarder must maintain extra state to rewrite reply names for multiple network regions.

Traceroute requests have the same privacy characteristics as regular Interests: observers can see that a client is requesting a particular name, but not who sent the request (since Interests carry no source address).
sections.plainLanguage: Bad actors could pretend to be a forwarder. To stop them, real forwarders sign their name in the reply. The client checks the signature to confirm it is real.
